prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Mary who mattered to me, gone or asleep among fruits, spilled in ash, in dust, I did not leave you. Even now I can't keep from composing you, limbs & blue cloak & soft hands. I sleep to the sound of your name, I say there is no Mary except the word Mary, no trace on the dust of my pillowslip. I only dream of your ankles brushed by dark violets, of honeybees above you murmuring into a crown. Antique queen, the night dreams on: here are the pears I have washed for you, here the heavy-winged doves, asleep by the hyacinths. Here I am, having bathed carefully in the syllables of your name, in the air and the sea of them, the sharp scent of their sea foam. What is the matter with me? Mary, what word, what dust can I look behind? I carried you a long way into my mirror, believing you would carry me back out. Mary, I am still for you, I am still a numbness for you.

Keywords: Mary, Even, Antique

outputs.L1:
Mary, who mattered to me—gone or asleep among fruits, spilled into ash, into dust—I did not leave you. Even now, I cannot keep myself from composing you: limbs, blue cloak, soft hands. I sleep to the sound of your name. I say there is no Mary except the word Mary, no trace upon the dust of my pillowslip. I dream only of your ankles brushed by dark violets, of honeybees above you, murmuring into a crown.

Antique queen, the night dreams on: here are the pears I have washed for you; here, the heavy-winged doves asleep beside the hyacinths. Here I am, having bathed carefully in the syllables of your name—in their air and sea, in the sharp scent of their sea foam.

What is the matter with me? Mary, what word, what dust can I look behind? I carried you a long way into my mirror, believing you would carry me back out. Mary, I am still for you; I am still a numbness for you.
outputs.L2:
Mary, you who were important to me—whether vanished or sleeping among fruit, scattered into ash and dirt—I never abandoned you. Even now, I cannot stop making you again in my mind: your body, your blue mantle, your tender hands. I fall asleep hearing your name. I tell myself there is no Mary beyond the sound of “Mary,” no mark left in the dust on my pillowcase.

I dream only of your ankles touched by shadowy violets, of bees hovering over you and humming as if shaping a crown. Ancient queen, the night continues its dreaming: these are the pears I rinsed for you; these are the doves with weighty wings, resting beside the hyacinths. And here I am, cleansed in the sounds of your name, immersed in their air and ocean, in the biting fragrance of their foam.

What is wrong with me? Mary, what word, what dust can I search beyond? I brought you deep into my reflection, trusting that you would lead me out again. Mary, I remain here for you. For you, I am still a kind of numbness.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker who mourns Mary’s absence while repeatedly insisting that she has not truly been abandoned. Although Mary is no longer physically present, the speaker continues to hold onto her with emotional intensity. This grief is not passive; it becomes an active effort to preserve Mary through thought, memory, and poetic expression. The speaker’s sorrow is shaped by the tension between loss and devotion: Mary is gone, yet the speaker refuses to let her disappear completely.

Throughout the poem, Mary is continually recreated through memory, language, and dreamlike imagery. The speaker does not recover Mary as a real, bodily presence, but instead rebuilds her imaginatively. She survives in fragments of speech, in repeated references to her name, and in the symbolic images that gather around her. In this sense, Mary becomes less a person who can be touched or seen and more an idea, a word, and an imagined presence sustained by the speaker’s longing. Her name itself carries emotional power, becoming a substitute for the physical trace that is missing.

The poem enriches this imagined presence by surrounding Mary with vivid and symbolic imagery. Images of fruit, flowers, doves, bees, sea foam, and royal beauty elevate her into an almost ideal or mythical figure. These images suggest sweetness, purity, fertility, delicacy, and majesty, creating a portrait of Mary that is intensely beautiful but also distant and unreal. The natural and dreamlike symbols do not simply describe her; they transform her into something radiant and unreachable. Mary becomes a figure shaped by desire and grief rather than by ordinary reality.

At the same time, the speaker’s devotion reveals a deep emotional paralysis. The repeated return to Mary suggests that the speaker is unable to move beyond the loss. Longing becomes a kind of trap, holding the speaker in a state of numbness, sorrow, and unanswered grief. The poem does not offer resolution or closure; instead, it shows a mind circling around absence, trying to fill it with words and images. Mary remains both present and absent: present in the speaker’s language and imagination, but absent in any physical or final sense. This unresolved tension gives the poem its emotional force, as the speaker continues to mourn, remember, and recreate Mary without ever truly recovering her.
outputs.L4:
The speaker’s address to Mary is shaped by mourning, longing, and obsessive repetition. Rather than simply remembering her, the speaker continually invokes her, as if saying her name might bring her back into being. Mary becomes the center of the poem’s language: she is called, imagined, offered gifts, and surrounded by dreamlike images. These images do not create a stable portrait of her; instead, they suggest that she can only be approached indirectly, through fragments of memory, sensation, and desire.

The poem’s repeated references to Mary show how grief turns language into ritual. The speaker seems to believe that words have a preserving power, that by naming Mary again and again he can keep her from disappearing completely. Sensory details and offerings deepen this effect. The speaker does not merely think about Mary; he tries to reconstruct her through touch, sight, sound, and symbolic gestures. These offerings become acts of devotion, attempts to give shape to someone who is no longer fully present.

At the same time, the poem recognizes the limits of this devotion. Mary is not truly restored by the speaker’s language. She exists mainly as a word, a name, and an absence. The more the speaker repeats her name, the more apparent it becomes that the name cannot replace the living person. Language preserves the memory of Mary, but it also emphasizes the distance between memory and reality.

As a result, the speaker’s love is both beautiful and painful. His devotion keeps Mary alive in the only way available to him, through speech and imagination. Yet this same devotion traps him in grief, because he cannot move beyond the absence he continually invokes. The poem therefore presents mourning as an act of creation and imprisonment at once: Mary is remade through language, but only as a haunting presence, never as a complete return.
outputs.L5:
Mary walked into the antique shop just as the evening light turned golden. Even before she opened the door, she could see shelves crowded with old clocks, silver mirrors, porcelain figures, and dusty books whose pages had yellowed with time.

At the back of the shop, Mary noticed an antique music box resting beneath a glass case. Even though it was small and plain, something about it caught her attention. The shopkeeper wound the tiny key, and a soft melody filled the room, delicate and haunting, as if it had been waiting many years to be heard again.

Mary smiled. She had come in only to look around, but she left with the antique music box wrapped carefully in brown paper, carrying with her a little piece of the past.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem addressed to a woman named Mary, blending grief, devotion, religious imagery, fruit, flowers, dust, and dreamlike surrealism.
counterfactuals.output:
Mary, I have carried your name in my mouth like a bruised plum, dark and sweet and splitting, and all day the bees of my grief have circled it. I do not know where to lay my sorrow, so I set it down among the lilies, beside the bowl of figs, beneath the small blue icon where the saints keep their patient, painted eyes open through the night.

Mary, the house is full of dust and annunciations. Dust on the windowsill, dust on the rosary, dust rising from the floorboards like the breath of vanished animals. When I kneel, it gathers on my knees as if I have been praying in a desert for forty years. When I stand, it follows me, a pale congregation, whispering your absence in the corners.

I dreamed you were walking through an orchard at dawn, the trees bent low with impossible fruit: pomegranates that beat like hearts, pears with golden mouths, apples filled with seawater and stars. You wore a crown of marigolds and your hands were luminous with pollen. Every blossom leaned toward you as though you were the first light ever made.

Mary, beloved, forgive me: I have mistaken grief for devotion, and devotion for a candle that never burns down. I have lit it before your face until the wax ran like milk, until the flame became a small red bird, until the bird flew into my chest and nested there. Now it sings only when I am sleeping.

At night the garden loosens from the earth and floats upward, roots trailing like wet hair. Roses drift past the moon. Violets open in the mouths of statues. A peach falls through the ceiling and breaks on the table, spilling its soft, sun-colored flesh over the letters I never sent you. I read the juice like scripture. It says: what is loved is never kept. It says: what is lost ripens elsewhere.

Mary, if heaven is real, let it be an apricot orchard after rain, with your footsteps filling slowly with light. Let there be bread on the sill, and hyacinths in a cracked jar, and dust made holy by the touch of your hem. Let me arrive there barefoot, carrying nothing but this devotion, this grief, this small basket of flowers gathered from the dream where you turned once, almost smiling, and called me by my secret name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic paragraph that repeats the name Mary and explores how a loved one survives only as language, with themes of memory, absence, mirrors, and longing.
counterfactuals.output: Mary, I say, and Mary returns only as breath against glass; Mary, I write, and the ink makes a small dark mirror where her face should be. In every room of memory, Mary is the chair left warm by absence, the window holding a sky I cannot touch, the echo that learns my mouth and answers from nowhere. Mary, Mary, Mary—the name becomes a rosary of longing, each syllable a bead worn smooth by grief, each repetition a way of keeping her from dissolving entirely. She survives not in the world but in the sentence, not in her hands but in the shape my hands make around her vanished name; and when I look into mirrors, it is Mary I almost see, Mary who flickers behind my eyes, Mary who is gone, and therefore everywhere language can still ache.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intimate, surreal love letter to Mary as if she is both a lost beloved and an icon, using ornate sensory details and a melancholic, devotional tone.
counterfactuals.output:
My dearest Mary,

I write to you from the blue hour, when the world loosens its gold clasp and everything beloved becomes unreachable.

Your name has been lying on my tongue all evening like a sugared relic, dissolving slowly, leaving behind the taste of rainwater, candle smoke, and the salt of an old wound. Mary—how softly the room changes when I say it. The walls bow inward as if to listen. The flowers in their vase turn pale with envy. Even the mirror dims, ashamed to reflect a face that is not yours.

I have loved you in so many impossible forms.

As a woman vanishing at the end of a platform, gloved hand raised, your eyes filled with farewell before the train had even arrived. As a saint in a chapel of cracked plaster, your painted heart pierced and shining, gathering the prayers of strangers like moths to a lamp. As the moon sinking into black water. As the last red fruit on a winter branch. As the silence after a choir has stopped singing, when the air still trembles with what cannot return.

Do you know what absence has made of you? It has dressed you in lapis and silver. It has lifted your face into every high window. I find you in the scent of bruised lilies, in the damp velvet of midnight, in the faint metallic taste of tears. Your absence has hands; it touches my hair while I sleep. It has a mouth; it whispers from the hollows of shells. It has eyes everywhere, and they are always looking away.

I keep a little altar for you in the country of my ribs.

There I place what remains: a ribbon the color of dried roses, a cup of milk gone cold, three matches, a black feather, the memory of your shoulder beneath my palm. I light imaginary candles until the whole cathedral of my body glows. I kneel before you, not because you are gentle, but because you are gone; and the gone are always holy. Loss has made a Madonna of you, crowned you with thorns of starlight, seated you above me in a heaven built from my own remembering.

If you returned, I think the earth would become too fragrant to bear. Bread would weep in the ovens. The sea would climb the stairs. Every clock would open like a pomegranate and spill its red, ruined time across the floor. I would not touch you at first. I would stand there, trembling like a votive flame, afraid that the slightest breath might turn you back into vision.

But if you spoke my name—only once, Mary, only once—I would come undone.

I would fall through all my years like a stone through water. I would be young again, and foolish, and full of that terrible brightness that comes before grief teaches the heart its manners. I would gather the hem of your dress in my hands as if it were scripture. I would press my face to it and find there the whole lost garden: wet leaves, warm figs, dust after rain, the animal sweetness of summer grass, your skin carrying the faint perfume of amber and sorrow.

Beloved, icon, wound, lamp—

forgive me for making a shrine of what was once simply human. Forgive me for polishing your memory until it no longer resembles mercy. I have only wanted to keep you from the rot of ordinary forgetting. I have only wanted some place where your beauty could go on breathing, even if that place was a chapel built from my loneliness.

Tonight the candles burn low. The sky is the color of old violets. Somewhere, bells are tolling for no one, or for me, or for the version of us that still walks hand in hand through a city made entirely of rain.

Receive this letter as you would receive a prayer placed beneath your painted feet.

Not to answer.

Only to know that I am still here, still faithful to the ache, still lifting my eyes to the blue distance where you have become both woman and star.

Yours in longing,  
always beneath your light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem about someone who cannot stop imagining Mary after her disappearance or death; include blue cloak, honeybees, dust, pillows, fruit, and the question “What is the matter with me?”
counterfactuals.output:
After Mary vanished, or died—no one could agree on the verb—I kept finding her in the ordinary weather of things. A blue cloak thrown over the back of a chair became the sea before rain. Honeybees worried the blossoms like tiny golden doubts. Dust rose from the road and made a body where there was none, shoulders, hair, the slight turn of her face away from me.

At night I pressed my mouth into the pillows and tasted salt, linen, the sleep of strangers. In the market, fruit split open under my thumb: figs dark as bruises, peaches giving up their sweetness too easily, pomegranates crowded with small red lamps. Everywhere, she was almost arriving. Everywhere, she had just left.

I began speaking to jars, doorways, the shadow beneath the table. I asked the bees if they had seen her. I asked the dust what it remembered. I asked the blue cloak, folded and refolded, to become a horizon and return her.

“What is the matter with me?” I said, and the room answered by filling itself with light. Not her light, perhaps. But close enough to wound me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
